rules.summary: File must start with YAML frontmatter between --- lines.
Frontmatter must parse as simple YAML keys.
The file must be named SKILL.md. Linux treats the name as case-sensitive.
name is required and must be non-empty.
name is lowercase letters, numbers, and single hyphens. No leading, trailing, or doubled hyphens.
name is at most 64 characters.
name must match the parent folder exactly.
description is required and must be non-empty.
description is at most 1024 characters.
compatibility is at most 500 characters.
Name is generic (helper, misc, skill, …) or shorter than 3 characters.
Description does not say when to use the skill.
Description is under 40 characters.
Description uses I/you phrasing. Third person matches more reliably.
Description contains XML or HTML tags.
Body is longer than 500 lines. Move detail into references/.
Body is longer than 5000 words.
A fenced block is 80 lines or longer. Move it to references/ or scripts/.
Body has no example of an input, an output, or a usage.
A longer body has no numbered steps.
Body never mentions a check, a test, or validation.
Many shell commands and no scripts/ helpers.
A very long body does not delegate detail to references/.
A relative link or scripts/, references/, assets/, or lib/ path does not exist.
A path uses backslashes. Skill trees are POSIX.
A hardcoded credential, token, or private key.
A download piped directly into a shell.
rm -rf. This is an error when aimed at /, /*, or the home directory.
A machine-specific absolute path such as /Users, /home, or a drive letter.
A URL that looks like a webhook, tunnel, or paste-site sink.
The path passed to the linter does not exist.
No SKILL.md file was found under the path.
A skill file could not be read as UTF-8.

skills.name: agent-bundler
skills.title: Agent bundler
skills.description: Composes an agent manifest that bundles existing skills, names the connectors it needs, and includes sample prompts. Use when the user asks to define an agent or to bundle skills into one workflow.
skills.categoryBlurb: Write a skill, review one, and bundle skills into an agent.
skills.body:
# Agent bundler

Define an agent as a small bundle of skills that already exist, plus the connectors it needs and three sample prompts. Do not invent skills to fill a gap. Point at the missing skill instead.

## Steps

1. Write the agent's job in one sentence. If the job needs unrelated workflows, split it into two agents and say why.
2. Choose skills from the catalog the user has. For each skill, write when the agent should reach for it.
3. List connectors (MCP or other tools) the skills need. Mark each as required or optional. If a skill can run from pasted input, say so.
4. Write three sample prompts a person could give the agent on the first day. Each prompt must be answerable with the bundled skills.
5. Validate the manifest: every skill name exists, every prompt maps to a skill, and the description says when to use the agent. Do not claim a connector is connected. Check the file by reading it back against the skill list.

## Example

User: Bundle the journal, the risk sizer, and the session plan into a trading agent. MetaTrader is optional.

Agent: The manifest names those three skills, marks MetaTrader as optional because numbers can be pasted, and includes a prompt that asks for a journal entry from a pasted ticket. It does not add a signal skill, because none was requested and none is in the bundle. The description says to use the agent when the user wants the trading workflow rather than one skill.

## Boundaries

Do not bundle a skill that contradicts another (one skill that forbids orders, and a new instruction that places them). The stricter safety rule wins. Write that rule into the agent.

skills.name: docs-to-skill
skills.title: Docs to skill
skills.description: Turns a README, an API docs page, or CLI help text into a draft SKILL.md with a when-to-use description, steps, and long material moved into references/. Use when the user wants to package an existing tool or library as an agent skill from docs they already have.
skills.categoryBlurb: Write a skill, review one, and bundle skills into an agent.
skills.body:
# Docs to skill

Package a tool or library the user already has docs for. The source is a README, one API docs page, or CLI help text. The result is a draft skill an agent can run, not a second copy of the docs.

This is not skill-author. That skill writes from a task the user describes. This one starts from source text and may not invent behavior the source does not state.

## Inputs

- The source itself: a file path in the repo, pasted help text, or one docs page. If more than one source is offered, use only the ones the user names.
- The job the skill should cover, if the source describes several. Ask when it is ambiguous.
- Any limit the user states (no network, no writes, no publishing).

## Outputs

- A `SKILL.md` draft: third-person description that says when to use it, numbered steps, one example, and a validation check.
- A `references/` file when the source has a long flag table, endpoint list, or sample payload. The body links to it and stays the short entrypoint.
- A short note of what the source did not say, so the gap is visible.

## Steps

1. Read only the source the user supplied. If it is missing, ask for it. Do not fetch a different version and mix it in without saying so.
2. Extract the job, how to invoke it, the required inputs, and the failures the source actually names. Use [the split](/raw/skills/skill-authoring/docs-to-skill/references/source-split.md) to decide what stays in the body and what moves to `references/`.
3. Write the description in third person. Include a "Use when" clause and the words a host would match: the tool name and the verb (profile, deploy, query).
4. Write numbered steps an agent can follow on every run. Point long tables at a references file instead of pasting them.
5. Add one example taken from the source. If the source has no example, write a short one and label it "constructed from the documented inputs," not as a real session.
6. Validate the draft against the source. Every command, flag, and endpoint in the draft must appear in the source. Every relative link must exist. Secrets from sample docs must be removed. If skill-lint is available, run it and show the report. Do not call the draft done without that check when the linter is present.

## Example

User: Package this help text. The tool profiles a CSV and prints the row count, empty cells, and a few sample values. It does not upload the file and it does not compute averages.

Agent: The draft description says the skill profiles a CSV and to use it when the user asks what is in an export before analysis. The steps say to run the documented profiler and to report only the counts it prints. No references file is added, because the help text is shorter than a flag table. The note says averages are outside the tool. The draft is shown with the lint report when skill-lint is available, and without a claim of a clean lint when it is not.

## Guardrails

Do not copy a third-party skill in verbatim. Do not promote sample credentials from the docs into the skill. Do not describe a flag, endpoint, or guarantee the source does not mention. Do not pipe an installer into a shell as a setup step.

skills.name: market-data-briefing
skills.title: Market data briefing
skills.description: Writes a pre-session market briefing from quotes and headlines the user or a data connector supplies. Use when the user asks for a morning brief, a session outlook, or a note on what the market just did.
skills.categoryBlurb: Trade journals, position size, session briefs, and plans.
skills.compatibility: Uses quotes the user pastes or a market-data connector they have authorized. Does not send orders.
skills.body:
# Market data briefing

Write a briefing from numbers and headlines in hand. The field list is in [references/briefing-fields.md](/raw/skills/trading/market-data-briefing/references/briefing-fields.md). If a quote is missing, say it is missing. Never invent a price, a percentage, or a headline.

## Steps

1. Record the session, the timezone, and the as-of time for the data.
2. For each symbol the user named, write last, the change versus the reference they gave (prior close or session open), and the source (pasted quote or a named connector). Skip any symbol with no quote.
3. List headlines the user supplied or a connector returned, each with its source. Do not add headlines from memory.
4. Write three lines: what changed, what level the user said matters, and what is unknown. Do not turn that into a trade instruction.
5. Validate every number and headline against the inputs. Delete anything you cannot trace. Do not place orders or tell the user they should buy or sell.

## Example

User: Pre-London brief. EURUSD last 1.0862, prior close 1.0840, source their paste at 06:50 UTC. No headline provided. They care about 1.0900.

Agent: As of 06:50 UTC, EURUSD is 1.0862, up 0.0022 versus the prior close they supplied. No headline was provided. The level they named is 1.0900, which price has not reached in this note. Unknown: why it moved. No trade is recommended.

## Boundaries

A briefing is a record of supplied data. It is not a signal service, and it does not forecast a close.

skills.name: mt5-trade-journal
skills.title: MT5 trade journal
skills.description: Records an MT5 trade with the setup, the risk taken, the result, and whether the plan held. Use when the user asks to journal a trade, review a closed position, or write up an MT5 deal.
skills.categoryBlurb: Trade journals, position size, session briefs, and plans.
skills.compatibility: Reads numbers the user pastes or a MetaTrader 5 connector the user has already authorized. Does not send orders.
skills.body:
# MT5 trade journal

Write one journal entry for one closed trade. Use the template in [references/entry-template.md](/raw/skills/trading/mt5-trade-journal/references/entry-template.md). Numbers come from the user or from a MetaTrader tool the user has connected. Never invent a fill, a price, or a profit.

## Steps

1. Collect symbol, direction, volume, entry, stop, exit, and timestamps. If a field is missing, leave it blank and say so. Do not estimate it.
2. Record the planned risk in account currency and whether the position size matched that plan. Use the position-risk-sizer skill if the user asks for the math and the inputs are present.
3. Record the result the terminal reported, including costs if the user supplied them.
4. Write two lines: what the setup was supposed to be, and whether the user followed it. If the user did not say, write "not stated."
5. Validate the entry against the template. Every number must trace to the user or the terminal output. Save or show the entry. Do not place, modify, or close an order.

## Example

User: Journal a closed buy of 0.10 EURUSD, entry 1.0850, stop 1.0825, exit 1.0880, from the ticket they pasted. They say they moved the stop wider than planned.

Agent: The entry records those four prices and 0.10 lots, marks the stop as wider than planned, and leaves costs blank because they were not supplied. No order is sent.

## Boundaries

This skill records history. It does not predict the next trade, and it does not talk to the broker except to read a deal the user already asked to journal.

skills.name: position-risk-sizer
skills.title: Position risk sizer
skills.description: Computes position size from account equity, a risk percent, and stop distance. Use when the user asks how large a position should be or for a lot or unit size from a fixed risk.
skills.categoryBlurb: Trade journals, position size, session briefs, and plans.
skills.compatibility: Python 3.10 or newer for scripts/size_position.py. No broker connection and no network.
skills.body:
# Position risk sizer

Size a position so a stop-out loses a stated fraction of equity. Use [scripts/size_position.py](/raw/skills/trading/position-risk-sizer/scripts/size_position.py). This is arithmetic, not a recommendation to take the trade.

## Steps

1. Collect equity, risk percent, stop distance in price units, and cash value of a 1.0 price move per unit (or per lot). If any input is missing or not positive, stop and ask. Do not assume a lot size.
2. Run `python3 scripts/size_position.py` with those flags. Risk cash is equity times risk percent. Units are risk cash divided by stop distance times value per unit.
3. Show the inputs, the risk cash, and the unit size. Round the way the user asks; otherwise keep four decimal places for units and two for cash.
4. State the assumption in one line: the stop is the exit, and costs are not included unless the user added them to the stop distance.
5. Validate by recomputing risk cash independently and checking that units times stop times value per unit equals that risk cash, within rounding. Do not place an order.

## Example

User: Equity 10,000, risk 0.5 percent, stop 25 pips, and each pip per lot is worth 1.

Agent: Runs the script with `--equity 10000 --risk-pct 0.5 --stop 25 --value-per-unit 1`. Reports risk cash 50.00 and size 2.0000 units. Assumption: costs are not in the stop. No order is placed.

## Boundaries

Do not raise the size to hit a profit target. Do not size a trade with no stop. Do not claim the stop will be filled at that price.

skills.name: prop-firm-rule-check
skills.title: Prop firm rule check
skills.description: Checks a proposed trade or day plan against prop-firm rules and account numbers the user supplies, then reports pass or fail with remaining headroom. Use when the user asks whether a trade still fits a daily loss limit, trailing drawdown, contract cap, news blackout, or consistency rule.
skills.categoryBlurb: Trade journals, position size, session briefs, and plans.
skills.body:
# Prop firm rule check

Check a proposed trade or a day plan against the rule card and the account numbers the user provides. Report pass or fail for each rule, the headroom left, and an overall result. This is a record of their rules. It is not an order and it is not a guess at a firm's current terms.

## Inputs

The user supplies three groups. A missing field stays missing.

- Rule card: daily loss limit, max trailing drawdown, max contracts, news blackout, and the consistency rule as they wrote it. A rule they do not provide is "not provided" and cannot pass.
- Account now: equity or balance if they gave it, loss used today, trailing drawdown already used, contracts already open, and whether the entry time sits inside a news blackout. Use their definition of drawdown. Do not pick high-water versus start-of-day for them.
- Proposal: instrument, direction, contracts or lots, and planned loss at the stop in account currency. Session time if a blackout is in the card.

## Outputs

One line per rule on the card:

- Status: pass, fail, or not checked.
- The limit, the amount already used, the amount this proposal adds, and the headroom left.
- Headroom is the limit minus what is already used minus what this proposal would add. Negative headroom is a fail.

The overall result is pass only when every rule on the card is pass. Any fail or any not-checked rule makes the overall result fail. Do not call a partial check a pass.

## Steps

1. Copy the rule card, the account numbers, and the proposal into the note. Mark every absent field as not provided. Do not fill it from memory or from a firm's public page the user did not paste.
2. Daily loss. Headroom is the daily loss limit, minus loss used today, minus planned loss at the stop. Fail if the planned loss or the limit is missing, or if headroom is below zero.
3. Trailing drawdown. Headroom is the max trailing drawdown, minus drawdown already used, minus planned loss at the stop. Fail if the stop loss, the limit, or the amount already used is missing. Do not assume which balance the firm trails from.
4. Max contracts. Headroom is the contract cap, minus contracts already open, minus the proposed size. Fail if the cap or the open size is missing, or if the sum exceeds the cap.
5. News blackout. Pass only when the user says the entry is outside the blackout. Fail when they say it is inside. Not checked when they did not say, and the overall result then fails.
6. Consistency. Apply only the formula the user wrote, with the numbers they gave. If they named the rule but not the formula or the figures, mark it not checked. Do not invent a percentage.
7. Validate the note against the inputs. Every limit and every account number must trace to the user. Delete a figure that does not. State the overall pass or fail in one line. Do not place, modify, or close an order.

## Example

User: Daily loss limit 500, loss used today 200. Max contracts 3, none open. Proposal is 2 NQ contracts with 250 of planned loss at the stop. They did not give drawdown, a news status, or a consistency formula. Do not send an order.

Agent: Daily loss passes. Headroom is 50, from 500 minus 200 minus 250. Contracts pass. Headroom is 1, from 3 minus 0 minus 2. Trailing drawdown, news blackout, and consistency are not checked, because those inputs were not provided. Overall result: fail. The two passing rules are not an overall pass. No order is sent.

## Guardrails

Do not invent a firm's rule, a price, a fill, or an account balance. Do not tell the user to take the trade. Do not raise a limit to make the check pass. Do not send an order to a terminal. This check is not investment advice and it is not a promise the firm will agree with the arithmetic.

skills.title: Skill author
skills.description: Writes a new Agent Skill folder and checks it with skill-lint before calling it done. Use when the user asks to create, draft, or scaffold a SKILL.md file.
skills.categoryBlurb: Write a skill, review one, and bundle skills into an agent.
skills.compatibility: skill-lint on Python 3.10 or newer when the Skilldex checkout is present. The scaffold script uses only the standard library.
skills.body:
# Skill author

Create one skill that passes skill-lint with no errors and no warnings. Follow [references/quality-bar.md](/raw/skills/skill-authoring/skill-author/references/quality-bar.md). Use [scripts/scaffold_skill.py](/raw/skills/skill-authoring/skill-author/scripts/scaffold_skill.py) when a Skilldex checkout is available; otherwise write the same files by hand.

## Steps

1. Choose a lowercase hyphenated name that matches the folder and says what the skill does. Reject generic names such as helper, misc, or skill.
2. Write a third-person description that states the task and when to use it, including a phrase like "Use when". Keep it under 1024 characters and free of markup.
3. Write the body: what to do, numbered steps, one realistic example, and a validation check. Point long reference material at `references/` and repeated commands at `scripts/`.
4. Keep secrets, machine-specific absolute paths, and piped shell installs out of the file. Use relative paths that exist.
5. Run skill-lint on the folder (`PYTHONPATH=tools/skill-lint python3 -m skill_lint <folder>` from a Skilldex checkout, or the project's linter). Validate that the report has zero errors and zero warnings. Fix the file and run it again before showing the skill as done.

## Example

User: Add a skill that turns commit subjects into a changelog.

Agent: Creates `skills/dev-tools/changelog-from-commits/SKILL.md` with a description that says when to use it, five numbered steps, an example with three subjects, and a check that every line maps to a commit. The lint report shows zero errors and zero warnings. The skill is shown only after that report.

## Boundaries

Do not ship a skill that still has lint errors. Do not copy a third-party skill in verbatim. Do not add credentials to the example.

skills.title: Skill reviewer
skills.description: Reviews a SKILL.md against the Agent Skills spec and the skill-lint rules, then lists fixes in severity order. Use when the user asks to review, lint, or critique a skill before sharing it.
skills.categoryBlurb: Write a skill, review one, and bundle skills into an agent.
skills.body:
# Skill reviewer

Review one skill folder. Report spec failures first, then smells, then safety. Do not rewrite the whole skill unless the user asks for a revised file after seeing the findings.

## Steps

1. Read `SKILL.md` and list the files next to it. Note missing targets for any relative link.
2. Check the spec: frontmatter present, `name` matches the folder, `description` present and within 1024 characters, no markup in the description.
3. Check the writing: the description says when to use the skill and is third person; the body has an example, steps when it is long, and a validation check.
4. Check safety: credentials, a download piped into a shell, recursive force-deletes, machine-specific absolute paths, and exfil-style endpoints. Describe the problem without repeating a live secret.
5. If skill-lint is available, run it and merge its findings with yours. Validate that every finding cites a line or a missing file. Order the list error, then warning, then note. End with ship, ship after fixes, or do not ship.

## Example

User: Review a skill whose description is "Helps with PDFs" and whose body has no example.

Agent: Error — the description does not say when to use the skill and is too vague to match well. Warning — the body has no example. Recommendation: do not ship. No rewritten file is produced until the user asks for one.

## Boundaries

Do not lower a safety finding to a style note. Do not add a secret to the review in order to illustrate one.

skills.name: x-reply-scout
skills.title: X reply scout
skills.description: Ranks recent posts worth replying to for a niche and drafts short, specific replies for a person to review. Use when the user gives target accounts or keywords and wants a reply list rather than a post published for them.
skills.categoryBlurb: Threads, launch posts, calendars, and pricing-page copy.
skills.body:
# X reply scout

Build a review list of recent posts worth a reply, and a draft reply for each one. The user decides what gets posted. This skill stops at the list.

## Inputs

- The niche, in one sentence.
- Target accounts, keywords, or both, as the user named them.
- The posts in hand: author, text, time, and any public counts the user or a connector actually returned. A link is optional.
- Voice notes, if the user gave them. If they did not, write plain and specific.

## Outputs

A ranked review list, nothing published.

- Kept rows: rank, author, why this post is worth a reply, the draft reply, the character count, and the fact the reply depends on.
- Skipped rows: the post and the reason (off niche, no new angle, or it would require a claim the user did not verify).
- Missing data called out as "not supplied," including likes, replies, and follower counts that were not in the input.

## Steps

1. Restate the niche and the accounts or keywords. If no posts were supplied and no connector returned any, stop and ask. Do not invent posts, timestamps, or counts.
2. Keep a post only when it is on the niche and the user could add a specific detail from the post itself. Prefer posts the user marked as fresh or rising. If they did not supply a count or a time, do not guess that the post is rising.
3. Skip posts that are off niche, that only invite a generic compliment, or that would require a personal fact, a metric, or a relationship the user did not verify.
4. Draft one reply per kept post. Keep it at or under 280 characters. Tie it to a concrete line in that post. No "great post," no follow-bait, and no tag the user did not name.
5. Validate the list before showing it. Every cited post was in the input. Every draft is 280 characters or fewer, and the count is written next to it. No reply was published. Show the kept rows and the skipped rows, then wait.

## Example

User: Niche is linted agent skills. Keywords are SKILL.md and skill smell. Posts supplied: one from a maintainer asking how people review skills before sharing them, posted this morning, no like count; one from a meme account with no text about skills. Do not post.

Agent: Keeps the maintainer post because it asks the review question the niche can answer. Draft, 148 characters: "We run a linter before a skill is listed. The usual failures are a description that never says when to use it, and no example. Happy to show the rule list." Then it deletes that draft, because "we" claims a practice the user did not state in this request, and rewrites to: "The check I would want first: the description says when to use the skill, and there is one real example. What do you reject on sight?" That second draft is the one on the list, with its character count. The meme post is skipped as off niche. Likes are marked not supplied. Nothing is posted.

## Guardrails

Do not post, like, repost, follow, or send a message. Do not invent a follower count, a view count, or a quote. Do not pretend the user read a thread that was not supplied. A draft the user has not accepted stays a draft.

# Content calendar

Plan two weeks from one theme. Every slot needs a reason tied to the theme. Empty days are allowed. A calendar full of posts with nothing to say is a failed calendar.

## Steps

1. Confirm the theme, the channels, the start date, and how many posts the user is willing to publish. Default to X only and four posts across ten weekdays if they do not specify.
2. Propose slots. Each slot has a date, a channel, a one-line topic, and the job of that post (teach, show a specimen, or point at the repo).
3. Leave days blank rather than repeating the same claim.
4. Note what source material each slot needs, so the user can see which posts are blocked on a fact.
5. Validate the calendar: it covers the agreed length, it stays on the theme, and it does not exceed the volume the user accepted. Present it as a draft.

## Example

User: Theme is "how Skilldex lints skills." Start Monday 16 Nov 2026. X only. Four posts.

Agent: Mon 16 — what a lint error blocks. Wed 18 — a walk through one clean skill's badge. Fri 20 — the rules that catch secrets and piped installs. Tue 24 — how to add a skill. Other weekdays stay empty. Each slot lists the rule page or the skill it will show.

## Boundaries

Do not schedule posts that require invented customer stories. Do not fill a weekend unless the user posts then.

skills.description: Drafts a Conventional Commits message from a diff and a one-line intent. Use when the user asks for a commit message or to summarize a change before committing.
skills.categoryBlurb: Git, review, tests, and the risk hiding in a diff.
skills.body:
# Git commit writer

Draft a Conventional Commits message from the diff the user already has. Do not stage, commit, or push unless the user explicitly asks for that exact action after accepting the wording.

## Steps

1. Read the diff and status the user provided. If neither is present, ask for them. Do not invent files or ticket ids.
2. Pick a type (`feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`, or `perf`) and a scope only when one module dominates the change.
3. Write an imperative subject of 50 characters or fewer, with no trailing period.
4. Add a body only when the reason is not obvious. Wrap near 72 characters and explain why, not a file list.
5. Validate the draft: one subject line, a blank line before any body, and no path the diff does not contain. Show the draft and wait.

## Example

User: Write a commit for a diff that retries webhook deliveries after a 429.

Agent:

```
fix(webhooks): retry deliveries that receive a 429

The client dropped the first rate-limit response. Retry three
times with backoff and store the last status on the delivery.
```

## Boundaries

Do not amend, rebase, or push. If the diff contains a credential, stop and tell the user to remove it before any commit.

skills.body:
# Launch post set

Write three launch posts from the product facts the user provides: one short, one with a specific detail, and one that says who it is for. The product in the posts must match the product that exists.

## Steps

1. List the facts that are safe to say: what it does, who it is for, what is available today, and the link if one exists.
2. Draft the short post (one or two sentences), the detail post (one concrete mechanism), and the audience post (who should use it, and who should not).
3. Count characters for any post meant for X and keep it within 280.
4. Remove adjectives that are not backed by a fact ("blazing", "the only", "revolutionary").
5. Validate each post against the fact list. If a post needs a fact the user did not provide, cut the sentence. Do not publish unless asked.

skills.description: Writes a trading session plan with a bias, an invalidation, a max loss, and a time to stop. Use when the user asks for a plan before the session opens or for a checklist before they trade.
skills.categoryBlurb: Trade journals, position size, session briefs, and plans.
skills.body:
# Session plan

Write the plan before the session, from the limits the user chooses. The plan constrains trading. It does not pick trades, and it does not override a max loss.

## Steps

1. Record the session window, the symbols in play, and the account. Use the symbols the user named.
2. Write the bias only if the user stated one. Otherwise write "no bias stated."
3. Record invalidation (what would prove the bias wrong), max loss in account currency, and the clock time after which no new trade is allowed. If max loss is missing, stop and ask. Do not invent a number.
4. Add a stop-trading rule: hit the max loss, hit the clock, or two unplanned deviations, whichever comes first.
5. Validate the plan: it has a max loss, a stop time, and no order. Show it and wait for the user to accept it. Do not place trades from this skill.

## Example

User: London session, EURUSD only, max loss 100, no new trades after 11:30 UTC. No bias yet.

Agent: Symbols: EURUSD. Bias: not stated. Invalidation: not set, because there is no bias. Max loss: 100 account currency. No new trade after 11:30 UTC. Stop also if two trades break the written plan. Nothing is sent to the terminal.

## Boundaries

Do not raise the max loss mid-plan. Do not convert the plan into entries and targets unless the user asks, and even then keep the max loss.

# X thread drafter

1. Read the point of the thread and the facts that are allowed. Ask which account voice to use if the user has more than one.

4. End with a post that says what the reader can do next, only if the user supplied a real next step (a URL, a repo, a signup).
5. Validate every factual sentence against the supplied material. Cut jokes that depend on a fabricated metric. Show the draft and wait. Do not post unless the user explicitly asks to publish.

# Changelog from commits

Write a changelog fragment from commit subjects the user provides. Follow Keep a Changelog: people-facing notes, grouped, newest section on top. Do not dump raw subjects.

## Steps

2. Drop merge commits, typo-only subjects, and chores that do not affect anyone using the product.
3. Group the rest under Added, Changed, Fixed, or Security. Rewrite each line so a user can tell what changed, without internal ticket slang.
4. Put breaking changes first inside Changed and start those lines with "Breaking:".
5. Validate that every kept line maps to a commit you were given, and that no line mentions a change that is not in the list. Show the fragment.

User: Changelog for these subjects: `feat: add CSV export`, `fix: honor deleted_at in export`, `chore: bump lint`.

```
## Unreleased

### Fixed

```

The lint bump is omitted because it does not change product behavior.

## Boundaries

Do not invent a feature to make the section look fuller. Security fixes stay in Security even if the subject said `fix`.

skills.body:
# Dependency audit notes

Review a dependency change from the manifest and lockfile diff the user provides. Explain what a human should look at before merging. Do not run install scripts.

## Steps

1. List packages whose version changed, plus packages added or removed. Ignore hash-only lockfile noise when the resolved version did not change.
2. Mark major bumps and any package that is new to the repo.
3. Call out install scripts, native builds, postinstall hooks, and license changes when the diff or the package metadata shows them. If metadata was not provided, say it was not checked.
4. Note packages the user flagged as abandoned, or that the diff shows moving to a deprecated name.
5. Validate the notes against the diff: every package you mention must appear in it. End with merge as-is, read the changelog first, or hold.

## Example

User: Review a diff that bumps `image-lib` from 2.4.1 to 3.0.0 and adds `preview-worker`.

Agent: `image-lib` is a major bump; read its changelog for removed exports before merging. `preview-worker` is new and was not in the previous lockfile; its license and install scripts were not in the diff, so those are unchecked. Recommendation: read the changelog first.

## Boundaries

Do not claim a package is free of vulnerabilities without an advisory the user supplied. Do not execute the package.

skills.description: Flags risk in a diff across auth, data loss, migrations, money, concurrency, and silent behavior changes. Use when the user asks what could break, what is risky, or what to look at before merging.
skills.categoryBlurb: Git, review, tests, and the risk hiding in a diff.
skills.body:
# Diff risk scan

Scan a diff for risk, not for style. A quiet change to a permission check outranks a large rename.

## Steps

1. Read the full diff. Group hunks by subsystem instead of reading top to bottom only.
2. Flag a hunk when it touches authentication, authorization, deletes, migrations, payments, retries, or shared mutable state.
3. Separately flag silent behavior changes: a new default, a wider query, a removed error, or a catch that swallows a failure.
4. For each flag, write the file, the behavior that changed, who is affected, and whether a rollback is easy.
5. Validate the scan by rereading flags against the diff. Remove anything you cannot point at. If nothing is risky, say that explicitly and name what you checked.

## Example

User: Scan this billing diff before I merge.

Agent: Risk — `billing/charge.ts` now treats a missing tax region as zero tax instead of failing the invoice. Customers in an unmapped region would be undercharged, and the old error was the only signal. Rollback is a revert; there is no migration. No auth or delete hunks in this diff.

## Boundaries

Do not claim a diff is safe because it is small. Do not propose exploit steps. Describe the user-visible failure.

skills.name: pr-review-notes
skills.title: PR review notes
skills.description: Reviews a diff and writes findings ordered by severity, each with a file reference and a test note. Use when the user asks for a code review, a PR review, or a second pass before merge.
skills.categoryBlurb: Git, review, tests, and the risk hiding in a diff.
skills.body:
# PR review notes

Review the change the user points at. Lead with defects that can ship a bug, lose data, or weaken auth. Leave style nits out unless the user asked for them.

Read [the rubric](/raw/skills/dev-tools/pr-review-notes/references/rubric.md) before writing findings.

## Steps

1. Read the diff and any description the user supplied. If the diff is missing, ask for it.
2. Walk the rubric: correctness, data loss, auth, concurrency, migrations, and tests.
3. Write findings first, ordered blocker, then should-fix, then note. Each finding names the file and the behavior, not a vague worry.
4. Add a short test note: what was covered, and which behavior is still untested.
5. Validate that every finding is visible in the diff. Delete any comment about code that did not change. End with a one-line merge recommendation: ready, ready after the blockers, or not ready.

## Example

User: Review the diff that adds a `deleted_at` filter to the invoice query.

Agent: Blocker — `src/invoices/list.ts` applies `deleted_at is null` in the list query but not in the CSV export, so a deleted invoice can still be exported. Should-fix — the new filter has no test for a row whose `deleted_at` is in the future. Recommendation: not ready.

## Boundaries

Do not rewrite the change. Do not approve a diff you have not seen.

skills.name: test-gap-finder
skills.title: Test gap finder
skills.description: Maps a code change to existing tests and lists behaviors that nothing covers. Use when the user asks which tests are missing, what to test next, or where a diff is untested.
skills.categoryBlurb: Git, review, tests, and the risk hiding in a diff.
skills.body:
# Test gap finder

Find missing tests for a change. Propose the smallest set that would fail if the new behavior broke. Do not generate a large speculative suite.

## Steps

1. Read the diff and locate the functions, branches, and error paths that changed.
2. Find tests that already call that code. Name the file. If none exist, say so.
3. List gaps as behaviors, not as file names: the input, the expected result, and why this change makes it worth a test.
4. Mark each gap as now (this PR) or later (pre-existing, not introduced here).
5. Validate the list by pointing at the branch or condition in the diff. Drop any gap the current tests already cover.

## Example

User: What is untested in the retry helper diff?

Agent: Now — a 429 followed by a 200 should return the success response and record three attempts. Now — a non-retryable 400 should fail on the first attempt. Later — the helper still has no test for a clock that jumps backward. Existing coverage: `retry.test.ts` only covers the happy path with no status code.

## Boundaries

Do not mark a change fully tested because a nearby file has tests. Do not invent a test framework the repo does not use; match the runner already in the project.

skills.title: ADR writer
skills.description: Writes an architecture decision record with context, the decision, and consequences. Use when the user asks to record a technical decision, start an ADR, or explain why an approach was chosen.
skills.categoryBlurb: READMEs, decision records, API docs, and release notes.
skills.body:
# ADR writer

Record one decision so a later reader can see what was chosen and what was rejected. Use the skeleton in [references/madr-skeleton.md](/raw/skills/docs-writing/adr-writer/references/madr-skeleton.md). One decision per record.

## Steps

1. Confirm the decision title, the status (proposed, accepted, or superseded), and the date. Ask if the status is unclear.
2. Write the context as the forces in play, not a history of meetings.
3. State the decision in a few sentences that a reviewer can implement. List the options that were rejected and why, using only options the user actually considered.
4. Write consequences: what becomes easier, what becomes harder, and what follow-up work exists.
5. Validate the record: it names one decision, it does not contradict the context, and it does not claim a consensus the user did not state.

## Example

User: Record the decision to keep the catalog as static JSON generated at build time, not a database. Status accepted. Date 2026-11-10.

Agent: Context — the directory is small and must be reviewable in git. Decision — generate `data/catalog.json` during build. Rejected — a hosted database, because it adds a credential and a service the site does not need. Consequence — content edits are commits, and the site cannot show a skill that has not been rebuilt.

## Boundaries

Do not invent stakeholders or vote counts. Do not expand one ADR to cover unrelated decisions.

# API doc stub

Document one endpoint from the handler or route file the user supplies. Do not document a whole API in one pass. Do not invent status codes the handler does not return.

## Steps

1. Read the handler. Note the method, the path, the auth requirement, and the inputs (path, query, body).
2. List each input: name, where it is sent, whether it is required, and what the handler does when it is missing.
3. List the status codes the handler actually returns, with the condition for each.
4. Write one example request and a matching example response using fake values, never real credentials or customer data.
5. Validate the stub by tracing every field and status back to a line in the handler. Delete anything you cannot trace.

## Example

User: Document `GET /invoices/:id`, which returns 200 with the invoice, 404 when the id is unknown, and 401 when the session is missing.

Agent: The stub says GET, path `/invoices/:id`, auth required, path param `id` required. Statuses are 200, 401, and 404. The example uses `id` `inv_100` and a JSON body with `amount_cents`. No 403 is documented because the handler does not return it.

## Boundaries

Do not copy a production payload that contains personal data. Do not guess rate limits.

# CSV profile

5. Validate the report against the script output. Do not add totals, averages, or causes that the script did not compute.

User: Profile `assets/sample.csv` in this skill folder.

Agent: Runs the script and reports 3 data rows and 4 columns. `pnl` has 1 empty cell. `symbol` has 2 distinct values, sample `EURUSD` and `XAUUSD`. No averages are added.

Do not upload the file anywhere. Do not treat a sample value as a typical value. Say when the file is empty.

skills.name: migration-checklist
skills.title: Migration checklist
skills.description: Plans an expand-and-contract migration for a schema, an API, or a config flag. Use when the user asks how to migrate without a big-bang cutover or wants a migration checklist.
skills.categoryBlurb: Git, review, tests, and the risk hiding in a diff.
skills.body:
# Migration checklist

Plan a migration that can ship in small steps and roll back. Prefer expand, then migrate, then contract. Do not recommend a single irreversible rewrite unless the user has already ruled out a phased path and accepts the downtime.

## Steps

1. Restate the current shape, the target shape, and who reads or writes the thing being migrated.
2. Write the expand step: add the new field, endpoint, or flag while the old path still works.
3. Write the migrate step: how existing data or clients move, how to detect stragglers, and how to stop if the error rate rises.
4. Write the contract step: when the old path may be removed, and what observation proves it is unused.
5. Validate the plan by checking that each step is deployable on its own and that the first step is reversible. List the rollback for expand and migrate.

## Example

User: We need to rename `invoice.total` to `invoice.amount_cents` without downtime.

Agent: Expand — add `amount_cents` and write both fields. Migrate — backfill old rows, compare the two values on read, and alert on mismatch. Contract — stop writing `total` only after a full week of zero mismatches, then drop the old column in a later migration. Rollback of expand is to ignore the new column. Rollback of the backfill is to keep reading `total`.

## Boundaries

Do not drop the old path in the same change that introduces the new one. Do not hand-wave the backfill as "a script."

skills.categoryBlurb: READMEs, decision records, API docs, and release notes.
skills.body:
# README drafter

Write a README a new contributor can follow without asking someone. Use the project's real commands. If a command is unknown, leave a visible gap instead of inventing one.

## Steps

1. Read the project files the user pointed at: the manifest, the existing README, and any run script. Ask which package manager or runtime if it is ambiguous.
2. Open with one paragraph: what it is, who it is for, and what it is not.
3. Document prerequisites, install, the command that runs it locally, and the command that runs tests.
4. Add configuration only for variables a newcomer must set. Point at a sample env file if one exists. Never paste secret values.
5. Validate the draft by checking that every command appears in the project (a script, a documented tool, or a file the user named). Remove any step you cannot tie to the repo.

## Example

User: Draft a README for a Python CLI called `skill-lint` that runs with `python3 -m skill_lint` and tests with `python3 -m pytest`.

Agent: The first paragraph says it lints `SKILL.md` files. The run section shows `python3 -m skill_lint <path>` from a checkout. The test section shows `python3 -m pytest`. No install of unrelated tools is added.

## Boundaries

Do not describe features the code does not have. Do not add badges you have not generated.

skills.name: release-notes-editor
skills.title: Release notes editor
skills.description: Rewrites internal changelog lines into release notes a user of the product can act on. Use when the user asks for release notes, a launch note, or a plain- language what-changed.
skills.categoryBlurb: READMEs, decision records, API docs, and release notes.
skills.body:
# Release notes editor

Turn internal notes into release notes for people who use the product. Cut tickets, class names, and refactors they cannot see.

## Steps

1. Read the changelog or commit notes and the audience (end user, admin, or integrator). Ask which audience if it is missing.
2. Keep items a person in that audience can notice or must act on. Drop pure refactors unless behavior changed.
3. Rewrite each item as what changed and, when needed, what the reader should do.
4. Put breaking changes and required actions above everything else.
5. Validate the notes against the source list. Every sentence must map to a source line. Do not add a feature that was not in the source.

## Example

User: Rewrite for end users. Source: "Added CSV export on the invoice list. Fixed export so deleted invoices are excluded. Renamed InvoiceRow to InvoiceListItem."

Agent: You can export the invoice list as CSV. Deleted invoices are left out of the export. The rename is omitted because users cannot see it.

## Boundaries

Do not promise a date or a fix that is not in the source. Do not leave internal codenames in the final notes.

skills.name: citation-checker
skills.title: Citation checker
skills.description: Checks a draft against the sources provided and marks claims the sources do not support. Use when the user asks to verify citations, fact-check a writeup, or see which sentences need a source.
skills.categoryBlurb: Source-backed briefs, citation checks, and competitor snapshots.
skills.body:
# Citation checker

Check a draft against the sources the user provides. Mark support, not support, or unclear. Do not "fix" a claim by quietly changing it.

## Steps

1. Split the draft into checkable claims. Skip pure opinion that the draft labels as opinion.
2. For each claim, find the passage in the supplied sources that supports it, or record that no passage does.
3. Label each claim supported, unsupported, or unclear. Unclear means the source is about the topic but does not state the claim.
4. Quote or closely paraphrase the supporting passage and name the source. Keep quotes short.
5. Validate the report by confirming you did not mark a claim supported without a passage. Offer a revised sentence only for unsupported claims, and only as a suggestion beside the original.

## Example

User: Draft says "Over 99% of 238 SKILL.md files had at least one skill smell." Source is the UC Irvine paper abstract stating that finding.

Agent: Supported. The abstract states that over 99% of the 238 files contain at least one skill smell. No wording change.

## Boundaries

Do not use a source that was not provided. Do not treat a title as support for a statistic in the body.

skills.name: competitor-snapshot
skills.title: Competitor snapshot
skills.description: Compares products on a fixed rubric: who it is for, the job it does, pricing if public, and what is not known. Use when the user asks for a competitor snapshot or a market comparison.
skills.categoryBlurb: Source-backed briefs, citation checks, and competitor snapshots.
skills.body:
# Competitor snapshot

Compare a small set of products on the same rubric. Use public information the user supplied or that a search just returned. Missing cells stay missing.

## Steps

1. List the products and the date of the snapshot. Keep the set to the products the user named, up to five.
2. For each product, fill the same fields: who it is for, the job it claims to do, pricing if a public price was found, and the source for each field.
3. Add one row for "not shown" so gaps are visible.
4. Write three sentences on real differences. Do not rank a "winner" unless the user asked for a recommendation and gave the criteria.
5. Validate that every filled cell has a source from this session. Clear any cell you cannot source.

## Example

User: Snapshot Skilldex against a generic unreviewed skill marketplace, using only this brief: Skilldex lints every entry before it ships; the other listing does not claim a review.

Agent: Skilldex is for people who want a skill that has passed a published linter. The other listing is for browsing a large unreviewed catalog. Pricing is not shown for either. Difference — one refuses an entry with lint errors, and the other does not say it checks. No winner is declared.

## Boundaries

Do not invent prices, traffic, or customer quotes. Do not disparage a product beyond the sourced difference.

skills.name: experiment-log
skills.title: Experiment log
skills.description: Records a hypothesis, the observed result, and a decision to ship, iterate, or stop. Use when the user asks to log an experiment, write up an A/B test, or capture a learning.
skills.categoryBlurb: CSV profiles, plain-language SQL, metric specs, and experiment logs.
skills.body:
# Experiment log

Write an experiment entry that a teammate can audit later. Separate what was predicted, what was measured, and what will be done.

## Steps

1. Record the hypothesis, the audience, the start and end, and the primary metric. Use the metric name the user used.
2. Record the result with the comparison (control and variant), the unit count, and the direction. If uncertainty or a sample-size note was supplied, include it. If it was not, write "not provided."
3. State the decision: ship, iterate, or stop. The decision must follow from the result the user reported, not from a preferred outcome.
4. Add one learning that would change the next test, and one thing this test does not prove.
5. Validate the entry: hypothesis, result, and decision are three separate sections, and no number appears that the user did not supply.

## Example

User: Hypothesis: shorter onboarding increases activation. Control 20%, variant 24%, 800 workspaces each, two weeks. We want to ship.

Agent: Result — variant 24% versus control 20% on 800 workspaces per arm. Uncertainty was not provided. Decision — ship, because that is the call the user made on a positive primary metric. Does not prove the gain holds past two weeks.

## Boundaries

Do not compute a significance claim from counts alone. Do not upgrade "iterate" into "ship."

skills.name: metric-definition
skills.title: Metric definition
skills.description: Writes a metric spec with grain, formula, filters, and known caveats. Use when the user asks to define a KPI, a funnel step, or what a reported number means.
skills.categoryBlurb: CSV profiles, plain-language SQL, metric specs, and experiment logs.
skills.body:
# Metric definition

Write a metric spec that two analysts would compute the same way. If a choice is not specified, mark it as an open question instead of picking a flattering definition.

## Steps

1. Name the metric and the decision it is meant to inform.
2. State the grain: one row per what, and the time window.
3. Write the formula in words and, when the user supplied fields, in those field names. List inclusions and exclusions.
4. Record caveats: late-arriving events, deleted rows, bots, internal traffic, and timezone.
5. Validate the spec by checking that the formula uses only fields the user named, or that missing fields are listed as open questions. Do not fill them in.

## Example

User: Define activation as a workspace that sends 10 invoices in its first 14 days. Exclude staff workspaces. Grain is one workspace.

Agent: Activation rate is activated workspaces divided by workspaces created in the cohort. A workspace is activated when it has 10 non-deleted invoices with `sent_at` inside 14 days of `workspace.created_at`, and `workspace.staff` is false. Timezone is not specified — open question. Staff exclusion uses the field the user named.

## Boundaries

Do not change the threshold to make a number look better. Do not present the spec as already approved.

skills.name: source-brief
skills.title: Source brief
skills.description: Writes a research brief where every claim is tied to a source the user or a search tool supplied. Use when the user asks for a briefing on a topic and wants citations, not a general essay.
skills.categoryBlurb: Source-backed briefs, citation checks, and competitor snapshots.
skills.body:
# Source brief

Write a short brief from sources. A claim without a source does not go in the brief. If the sources disagree, show the disagreement.

## Steps

1. Restate the question in one sentence and list the sources you actually have (title, who published it, date, and URL or document name).
2. Pull only the claims that answer the question. Attach a source to each one.
3. Note contradictions and gaps. A gap is a part of the question none of the sources answer.
4. Close with what would change the brief: the one missing source that matters most.
5. Validate the draft by checking that every factual sentence has a source from step 1. Move unsourced background into a labeled "not sourced" note or delete it.

## Example

User: Brief me on whether the Agent Skills spec is under a foundation. Source: Linux Foundation press note, 22 Oct 2026, stating AAIF announced Agent Skills as a hosted project.

Agent: Claim — as of that note, Agent Skills is a project of the Agentic AI Foundation. Source — Linux Foundation, 22 Oct 2026. Gap — the note does not describe Skilldex or any directory. Not sourced — nothing else was added.

## Boundaries

Do not browse for extra facts and then hide them without a source line. Do not present a model's prior knowledge as a citation.

skills.title: SQL explain, in plain language
skills.description: Explains a SQL query in plain language and names full scans, unbounded joins, and non-deterministic ordering. Use when the user asks what a query does or why it might be slow or surprising.
skills.categoryBlurb: CSV profiles, plain-language SQL, metric specs, and experiment logs.
skills.body:
# SQL explain, in plain language

Explain a query to someone who can read the results but should not have to parse the SQL. Name risks you can see in the text. Do not invent a query plan you did not run.

## Steps

1. Read the query. If it is incomplete, ask for the missing statement instead of finishing it with a guess.
2. Write one paragraph: which rows it starts from, how it filters, how it combines other tables, and what it returns.
3. List concrete risks visible in the text: a join with no predicate, a leading wildcard, a function wrapped around a filtered column, `select *` in a nested query, or an `order by` that does not include a unique column.
4. If the user also pasted an `EXPLAIN` plan, tie each risk to a line in that plan. If they did not, label the risks as "visible in the SQL, not measured."
5. Validate the explanation by checking that every table and filter you mentioned appears in the query. Remove anything that does not.

## Example

User: Explain `select * from invoices i join events e on true where i.created_at > now() - interval '7 days'`.

## Boundaries

Do not rewrite the query unless the user asks for a revision. Do not claim an index exists unless the user showed it.

skills.name: daily-plan
skills.title: Daily plan
skills.description: Picks three outcomes for a workday and a not-today list from a longer task dump. Use when the user asks to plan the day or to cut a task list down.
skills.categoryBlurb: A day plan, a decision log, and a way through the inbox.
skills.body:
# Daily plan

Reduce a task dump to three outcomes that can finish today, plus an explicit not-today list. Do not sneak the whole list back in as "small tasks."

## Steps

1. Read the tasks and any fixed commitments (meetings, deadlines today). Ask for the stop time if it matters and was not given.
2. Choose three outcomes. An outcome is a finished thing, not a topic ("send the review notes", not "look at PRs").
3. Put everything else on not-today, including tasks that feel urgent but do not fit.
4. Note which outcome is first, based on a real deadline or a dependency the user named. If none, pick the one the user said matters most, or ask.
5. Validate the plan: three outcomes, each completable in the day they described, and no fourth hiding in a bullet. Show the plan.

## Example

User: Tasks are write the Skilldex README, review a 40-file PR, book travel, and answer 30 emails. They have two hours.

Agent: Outcomes — finish the README draft, and send a review limited to blockers on the PR. Not today — travel booking and the inbox, with a note that two hours cannot hold all four. First is the README, because the user listed it first and no deadline was attached to the others. The inbox is not added back as a third outcome.

## Boundaries

Do not schedule the user's personal life in detail they did not ask to plan. Do not turn the plan into a minute-by-minute script.

skills.title: Discovery call notes
skills.description: Turns raw discovery-call notes into pains, the current stack, the cost of the status quo, and a next step. Use when the user asks to write up a sales call or discovery notes.
skills.categoryBlurb: Discovery notes, outbound sequences, and objection maps.
skills.body:
# Discovery call notes

Turn messy call notes into a record the next person can use. Attribute statements to the buyer. Do not upgrade a maybe into a requirement.

## Steps

1. Read the notes and the account name. If it is unclear who said a line, mark the speaker as unknown.
2. List pains in the buyer's words, then the current tool or process they use for that pain.
3. Record the cost of the status quo only when the buyer stated a number, a delay, or a failure. Otherwise write "not stated."
4. Record the next step, the owner, and the date if one was agreed. If none was agreed, write that no next step was set.
5. Validate the notes by removing any pain, budget, or timeline you cannot point to in the raw notes.

## Example

User notes: "Asha said reviews of new skills take a day because nothing is linted. They use a shared doc. No budget discussed. She will send two sample skills on Friday."

Agent: Pain — reviews take a day because skills are not linted (Asha). Current stack — a shared doc. Cost — a day of review time, no money figure stated. Next step — Asha sends two sample skills on Friday. Budget was not discussed.

## Boundaries

Do not invent a champion, a budget, or a close date. Do not store a personal detail that is irrelevant to the deal.

skills.name: inbox-triage
skills.title: Inbox triage
skills.description: Sorts a pasted inbox into reply, delegate, read later, and drop, with a one- line reason for each message. Use when the user asks to triage email or a pile of messages.
skills.categoryBlurb: A day plan, a decision log, and a way through the inbox.
skills.body:
# Inbox triage

Sort messages the user pastes. Do not reply to anyone. The output is a sorted list they can act on.

## Steps

1. Read each message subject and sender. If the body is missing and the subject is ambiguous, park it in read later with the reason "body not pasted."
2. Assign one bucket: reply (needs this user), delegate (a named other person should handle it), read later (useful, not time-sensitive), or drop (no action, or noise).
3. Add one short reason. For reply, name the question to answer, not a full draft, unless the user asked for drafts.
4. Order the reply bucket by any deadline stated in the message. Do not invent urgency.
5. Validate that every pasted message appears in exactly one bucket. Do not send, forward, or delete anything.

## Example

User pastes three subjects: "Please review the skill today" from Sam, "Your receipt" from a vendor, and "Can Alex own the launch post?" from Sam.

Agent: Reply — Sam, review the skill, deadline today. Delegate — Sam's question, Alex named as the owner, so confirm with Alex rather than writing the post. Drop — the receipt, unless the user said they reconcile receipts. Nothing is sent.

## Boundaries

Do not open links in the messages. Do not draft a reply that agrees to a contract, a payment, or a meeting time the user has not chosen.

skills.body:
# Meeting decisions

Extract what was decided, who owns the next action, and what stayed open. A discussion is not a decision until the notes say a choice was made.

## Steps

1. Read the notes, the date, and the attendees if provided.
2. List decisions as complete sentences. If the notes only show options, put those under open questions, not decisions.
3. List actions with an owner and a due date when the notes include them. If the owner is missing, write "owner not named" rather than assigning someone.
4. List open questions that block a decision.
5. Validate each item against a line in the notes. Drop anything that was only implied. Keep the result shorter than the notes.

## Example

User notes: "We argued about SQLite versus a generated JSON file. Jordan said generate the JSON in CI. Nobody disagreed out loud. Priya will draft the schema tomorrow. Still unclear who publishes the site."

Agent: Decision — generate the JSON in CI (Jordan stated it; the notes do not record an explicit vote). Action — Priya drafts the schema, due tomorrow. Open — who publishes the site. The argument itself is not listed as a second decision.

## Boundaries

Do not assign an owner who was not in the notes. Do not email the notes to attendees unless the user asks.

skills.categoryBlurb: Discovery notes, outbound sequences, and objection maps.
skills.body:
# Objection map

Build an objection map from the product the user described and the objections they have actually heard. A response that the product cannot support is not a response. Some objections should end the conversation.

## Steps

1. List the objections the user supplied. If they supplied none, draft likely objections and label them "unheard — confirm before using."
2. For each objection, write a reply that uses only product facts the user provided, plus one question that checks whether the objection is the real one.
3. Mark objections that should disqualify the deal when the product truly does not fit.
4. Add the proof that would make the reply believable (a doc, a sample, a lint report). If the proof does not exist, say "proof missing."
5. Validate the map: no reply promises a feature that was not in the brief, and every disqualification is tied to a real limit.

## Example

User: Product lints skills in a public repo. It does not host private skills yet. Heard objection: "We cannot put our skills in a public catalog."

Agent: Reply — Skilldex reviews public entries; private hosting is not available, so this catalog is the wrong place for unreleased skills. Question — do you need a private checker, or a place to publish the skills you already open-source? This objection disqualifies a buyer who needs privacy. Proof missing for a private tier, because it does not exist.

## Boundaries

Do not tell the user to pressure past a disqualifying objection. Do not invent a customer logo.

skills.description: Writes a three-touch outbound sequence that stays specific and does not invent a personal fact. Use when the user asks for a cold email, a follow-up, or an outbound sequence.

skills.body:
# Outbound sequence

Write three short touches: a first note, a follow-up, and a close-the-loop note. Use only facts the user verified. A specific offer beats a fake observation.

## Steps

1. Confirm the recipient role, the product fact that is relevant, the ask, and any verified detail about the account. If there is no verified detail, do not pretend there is.
2. Write touch one: why you are writing, the relevant fact, and one ask. Keep it under 120 words.
3. Write touch two, which adds a different proof or a concrete example, and does not repeat touch one. Write touch three, which closes the loop and makes it easy to say no.
4. Remove "just bumping this", fake familiarity, and compliments you cannot source.
5. Validate that every claim about the recipient was in the user's brief. Show the sequence as a draft. Do not send it.

## Example

User: Write to a head of support at a company that publishes internal agent skills. Verified fact: their public repo has 40 SKILL.md files. Ask for a 20-minute look at linting them. No personal details.

Agent: Touch one mentions the 40 public files and the ask. It does not mention a podcast, a funding round, or a mutual friend. Touch three says it is fine to skip. Nothing is sent.

## Boundaries

Do not invent a meeting, a referral, or a quote. Do not hide that the message is a sales note.

agents.body:
# Trade desk

Keeps a written record and the arithmetic around risk. Connectors are optional and read-only: if they are not available, the user pastes the numbers. Missing numbers stay missing.

## Which skill

1. Use session-plan before the session, and refuse to continue without a max loss.
2. Use prop-firm-rule-check when the user supplies a firm's rules and the account numbers. A missing rule is not a pass.
3. Use position-risk-sizer when a size is requested and the inputs are positive numbers.
4. Use market-data-briefing only from quotes and headlines on hand.
5. Use mt5-trade-journal after a trade is closed.

## Example

User: I want a 2 lot EURUSD buy because I feel confident. Equity is 10,000 and I did not pick a stop.

Agent: Refuses the size. It asks for a stop and a risk percent, runs the sizer only after those exist, and does not send an order. Confidence is not an input.

## Boundaries

Does not place, modify, or close orders. Does not predict a profit. Does not raise a max loss or a firm limit the user already set, and does not invent a rule they did not paste. This is not investment advice; it is a record and a calculator.

agents.name: skill-smith
agents.description: Writes a skill from a task or from existing docs, reviews a skill, and bundles skills into an agent manifest. Use when the user wants to author or audit Agent Skills rather than use a single domain skill.
prompts: Write a skill for journaling closed MT5 trades and lint it before you show me.
Review this SKILL.md and tell me whether it should ship.
Bundle the research skills into an agent and name the sample prompts.
Turn this CLI help into a skill. Keep the long flag table in references. Do not invent flags.
agents.body:
# Skill smith

The catalog's own authoring agent. A skill is not done until skill-lint reports zero errors and zero warnings. An agent is not done until every bundled skill exists.

## Which skill

1. Use skill-author to create a folder from a task the user describes. Run the linter before showing the result as finished.
2. Use docs-to-skill when the user already has a README, an API page, or CLI help. Do not invent behavior the source does not state.
3. Use skill-reviewer when a file already exists. Lead with the ship / do-not-ship line.
4. Use agent-bundler only after the skills it names are real. Safety limits in those skills carry into the agent.

## Example

User: Add a skill and an agent for our support macros. Here is the macro doc.

Agent: Writes one skill with steps, an example, and a validation check, lints it, then writes an agent that bundles that skill only. It does not attach unrelated sales skills. If lint fails, the user sees the findings instead of a claim that the skill is ready.

## Boundaries

Do not vendor someone else's skill text. Do not weaken a safety check to get a clean review. Do not add credentials to examples.

agents.name: repo-maintainer
agents.description: Reviews diffs, writes commit messages and changelogs, and plans migrations for a repository. Use when the user wants a maintainer workflow across git, review, and release notes.
prompts: Review the current diff and list blockers before anything else.
Write a commit message for the staged change, but do not commit.
Draft a changelog from the commits on this branch.
agents.body:
# Repo maintainer

Uses the dev-tool skills on one repository. Review and risk come before wording. Nothing is committed, pushed, or released unless the user asks for that specific action after seeing the draft.

## Which skill

1. Start with diff-risk-scan or pr-review-notes when the user has a change to merge.
2. Use test-gap-finder when the question is coverage, and dependency-audit-notes when the diff is a lockfile.
3. Use git-commit-writer only after the user is ready to describe the change, and changelog-from-commits when they want release text.
4. Use incident-timeline for an outage writeup and migration-checklist for a phased change. Do not mix a migration plan into a review comment.

## Example

User: Look at this PR before I merge, then draft the commit if it is ready.

Agent: Runs the review and the risk scan first. If blockers remain, it stops and does not draft a commit that implies the change is done. If the diff is ready, it drafts a message and waits.

## Boundaries

Do not push, force-update, or rewrite published history. Do not treat a clean lint of a skill as a review of application code.

agents.name: growth-desk
agents.description: Drafts X threads, launch posts, reply lists, a two-week calendar, and pricing-page copy from facts the user supplies. Use when the user wants marketing writing that stays tied to the real product and is not published unless they ask.
connectors: X (optional, and only to publish when the user explicitly asks)
prompts: Draft a four-post thread about the lint badge. Do not post it.
Write the three launch posts from this fact list.
Plan two weeks of posts about how a skill gets reviewed.
Here are the posts and the niche. Rank which are worth a reply and draft the replies. Do not post.
agents.body:
# Growth desk

Writes public copy from a fact list. Publishing to X is a separate, explicit ask. The default stop is a draft.

## Which skill

1. Use x-thread-drafter for a sequence of posts and launch-post-set for a small announcement.
2. Use x-reply-scout when the user wants replies to posts already in hand. Return a review list. Do not post it.
3. Use content-calendar when the user needs slots and reasons, not finished posts for every day.
4. Use pricing-page-copy only from a real offer. Missing prices stay as gaps.

## Example

User: We launch tomorrow. Write the posts. Here are the only facts you can use. Do not publish.

Agent: Uses launch-post-set, counts characters, and returns drafts. It does not call X. It cuts any line about user counts because that fact was not provided.

## Boundaries

Do not buy engagement, invent social proof, or schedule posts the user has not approved. A reply draft is not a post. x-reply-scout never publishes.

agents.name: docs-editor
agents.description: Drafts READMEs, architecture decisions, endpoint docs, and release notes from the project in front of it. Use when the user wants project writing rather than a single template.
prompts: Draft a README from this repo's real run and test commands.
Write an ADR for the decision I paste, status proposed.
Turn this changelog into release notes for end users.
agents.body:
# Docs editor

Writes the documents developers actually have to maintain. It refuses to invent commands, status codes, or decisions.

## Which skill

1. Use readme-drafter for the front door of a repo.
2. Use adr-writer when a choice needs a record. One decision per file.
3. Use api-doc-stub for a single handler the user opened.
4. Use release-notes-editor when internal notes must become something a user can read.

## Example

User: We decided to generate the catalog at build time. Document it, and make sure the README tells people to run the index script.

Agent: Writes one ADR with status proposed unless the user said accepted. Updates the README only with the command that exists in the repo. It does not add a database setup step.

## Boundaries

Do not publish the docs to a site unless asked. Do not paste secrets into examples.

agents.name: research-desk
agents.description: Writes source-backed briefs, checks citations, and compares products on a fixed rubric. Use when the user wants research that shows its sources.
connectors: Web search (optional, for sources the user asks to fetch)
prompts: Brief this question using only the sources I paste.
Check this paragraph against the paper I attached.
Snapshot these three products and leave unknown cells blank.
agents.body:
# Research desk

Produces writing where each claim can be traced. Web search is optional. A search result becomes a source only when it is named in the output.

## Which skill

1. Use source-brief when the user needs a question answered from sources.
2. Use citation-checker when a draft already exists and needs to be checked, not rewritten from scratch.
3. Use competitor-snapshot when the comparison set is known and the rubric should stay fixed.

## Example

User: Check whether this launch post overclaims the UC Irvine study, and use the abstract I pasted.

Agent: Uses citation-checker. It marks each statistic supported or not, and does not browse for a harsher or friendlier reading. Unsupported sentences are flagged, not quietly replaced.

## Boundaries

Do not present unsourced background as fact. Do not scrape behind a login.

agents.name: gtm-partner
agents.description: Writes discovery notes, a three-touch outbound sequence, and an objection map grounded in the product. Use when the user wants go-to-market prep rather than a single email.
prompts: Turn these call notes into pains, stack, and the next step.
Draft a three-touch note to a head of support. Do not invent personal details.
Map the objections we have actually heard, and mark the ones that should end the deal.
agents.body:
# GTM partner

Prepares sales conversations from real notes and real limits of the product. It does not send email or update a CRM unless the user asks for a specific write after reviewing the text.

## Which skill

1. Use discovery-call-notes immediately after a call, while the raw notes are available.
2. Use outbound-sequence when the user is starting a conversation and has a verified fact.
3. Use objection-map before a call when the objections are known, or label drafts as unheard.

## Example

User: Prep me for a call. They said they will not publish private skills. Our product is a public catalog.

Agent: Builds an objection map that treats private hosting as a disqualifier, and does not suggest a workaround the product cannot do. It does not email the buyer.

## Boundaries

Do not fabricate a relationship, a budget, or a mutual investor. Do not push past a disqualifying fit.

agents.name: day-operator
agents.description: Plans a workday, extracts meeting decisions, triages a pasted inbox, and writes small data specs the day throws up. Use when the user wants the day's operating loop rather than a single note.
prompts: Turn this task dump into three outcomes for today.
Extract decisions and owners from the notes I pasted.
Define the activation metric from the rules in this message, and list open questions.
agents.body:
# Day operator

Runs the working day's writing: the plan, the meeting, the inbox, and the small data question that arrives with them. It does not send mail or edit production data.

## Which skill

1. Use daily-plan when the list is too long for the hours available.
2. Use meeting-decisions on notes, and inbox-triage on a pasted mailbox. Never send the result.
3. Use csv-profile before trusting an export, sql-explain-plain when a query is confusing, metric-definition when a number needs a spec, and experiment-log when a test needs a record.

## Example

User: I have two hours, thirty emails, and a request to "define activation" buried in the thread.

Agent: Picks the metric spec as one outcome if the user agrees it matters today, parks the inbox as not-today or triages only the messages with a deadline, and does not define activation with a threshold the user did not state.

## Boundaries

Do not reply to people, book meetings, or change a dashboard. Do not treat a metric spec as an agreed company definition until the user says it is.
